div.p: This article describes a study to assess the accessibility of the contents concerning the websites of 20 universities from all around the world. The accessibility assessment was carried out to verify compliance with the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.0 (WCAG 2.0) published by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C). The main goal of this study is to determine if even people with disabilities can access and use websites of the universities with higher academic prestige. Besides, in our approach we also make use of the Website Accessibility Conformance Evaluation Methodology (WCAG-EM) is an approach for determining how well a website conforms to WCAG 2.0. The WCAG-EM provides a guidance on using the methodology and considerations for specific situations.

From the results, we can conclude that the majority of the tested websites do not achieve an acceptable level of compliance. Universities with high academic prestige do not show a greater level of web accessibility. By performing the evaluation of university websites, we have identified that there are major barriers to a large number of users.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The web accessibility indicates the ease of admission to websites to all public, especially to those with disabilities, to access a product or service. Web accessibility allows entering to the websites so that all users can perceive, understand, navigate and interact with the web [1]. The Web in its origin was purely a text-based medium; however, when the Web started to be used also as a commercial platform, design and visual appearance became more important [2]. During that process, most web developers did not apply suitable designs for universal access; therefore, the Web became less and less usable for people with disabilities. In the last years, people got aware of this problem, and the keyword "Web accessibility" has become rather popular [3]. 1 http://www.webometrics.info/es This paper presents an analysis of web accessibility content established by the recommendation of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.0 (WCAG 2.0) [4]. The analysis was applied to the main page of 20 worldwide universities ranked by Webometrics 1 . The accessibility assessment was carried out to verify compliance with accessibility guidelines of the selected universities. If the main page is not accessible, users may have trouble accessing to other pages of the site. This preliminary study will allow universities to comply with accessibility guidelines.

It should be noted that there are some studies related to websites accessibility. In the case of Spanish universities [5] the results of websites accessibility of ten Andalusian Universities presented in the study, indicated that there are many ways to achieve full accessibility.

In the case of usability and accessibility to the content of websites of major US Universities [6], the results showed that there is 30% compliance with relation to web accessibility guidelines. Regarding the study of web accessibility policies in Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) [7], studies have indicated that a large number of the websites of schools and university libraries are not accessible. These findings have caused concern and have reflected that there is so much to do in terms of the accessibility of websites.

Regarding to the article related with the accessibility of websites from Turkish universities [8], the results from assessing the level of accessibility to the examined web sites, show that a large number of websites have accessibility problems. The study suggests that it would be a good practice to adopt the principle of simple web design, using open source and management systems of free content. However, it recommends that universities hire an outside firm that specializes in the problems of web accessibility, in order to realize audits of the case.

In universities of South America, there is a web accessibility study from Universidad de las Fuerzas Armadas-ESPE [9]. This study confirms that there are studies of web accessibility available for evaluation of the web accessibility in higher education. There are also studies of government sites of South America [10]. In both cases, the results indicates that the websites do not provide adequate levels of accessibility.

Studies on government website the mobile websites of different countries and the experience of browsing of users, suggests that the websites should be designed for all types of mobile devices and operative systems. [11]. These sites must be accessible to all, regardless of their abilities, which is suggested to apply the guidelines WCAG 2.0.

There are also studies about the performance of webbased on metrics for evaluating reliability and maintainability of hypermedia applications, which recommend applying web page replacement algorithms for increasing the website usability, maintainability, reliability, and ranking [12].

The rest of this paper is structured as follows: section II explains some basic concepts about web accessibility; section III presents the method applied in the analysis; section IV shows an analysis of the results; and lastly, in section V the conclusions obtained in the analysis were established.

div.head: II. ACCESSIBILITY
div.p: WCAG 2.0 are divided into four general principles, organized into 12 guidelines [13]. The principles of WCAG 2.0 are the following:

1. Perceivable: the criteria allow the product to be perceivable by people, regardless of their disabilities. 2. Operable: the user interface components and navigation must be operable. 3. Understandable: the information and the operation of user interface must be understandable. 4. Robust: the content must be robust enough that it can be interpreted reliably by a wide variety of user agents, including assistive technologies.

The guidelines are composed of compliance criteria; each criterion has an adequacy level of conformity that can indicate the impact of accessibility. A number of requirements must be observe in order to comply a website with the WCAG 2.0 guidelines. Three levels are identified: 1. Level A: this is the minimum level. 2. Level AA: this is the middle level; the website must meet all the criteria under levels A and AA. [14]. This method proposed the evaluation of all types of static and dynamic websites, mobile versions, etc.
As such, this study presents a method to guide to evaluators in order to promote good practices, improve and replace the requirements outlined in WCAG 2.0.

In this method it is essential the knowledge provided by the expert on the WCAG 2.0. The evaluator must understand web technologies, accessibility barriers, techniques, tools and evaluation methods to identify such limitations.

The method is flexible and it can be applied in different situations and contexts, such as self-evaluation, evaluation by third parties, evaluation during development, periodic evaluations, etc. The diagram presented in Fig. 1 shows the five phases applied in the evaluation of websites in this work. The study measured aspects of the site as the type of web pages, the size, complexity, the technologies used, and the knowledge of experts to design and develop the websites.
Phase 1: Define the evaluation scope In the first phase, it is necessary to define the scope of the site, the pages to which will be applied the evaluation.

Aspects and developed services, versions of it, parts of the portal should be documented Furthermore, the adequacy level (A, AA, AAA) [14] to be evaluated is defined. This study applied the level of conformity AA. A list of used web browsers and products of support with accessibility features should be defined too.

Phase 2: Explore the target website The purpose of phase two is to determine the features that are essential for a website. Within the site, there may be many pages and page states with different styles, designs, structures and functions.

Probably, these pages have been generated using different templates or written by different people. In this phase, the expert reviews the website, in order to check for broken links, detects the most important pages of the website. Besides, the expert also examines and analyzes the web pages for key information.

Phase 3: Select a sample In phase three, the main page of each university is identified. Previously the states of the websites that were not part of the sample were reviewed, but which acted as indicators of verification of results. Phase 4: Audit sample In phase four, each sample site is verified in order to meet with compliance requirements and the adequacy level AA concerning WCAG 2.0. In assessing was verified the functionality of the processes, the introduction of data, notifications and interactions.
Phase 5: Record results At last, in phase five the results are documented. This documentation is generated in each process to justify and ensure transparency and reproducibility of the analysis.

div.head: IV. ANALYSIS OF RESULTS
div.p: At present, there are several tools available for assessment and verification of web accessibility, to automate the process of evaluating the accessibility of the web pages and value the level of compliance. The majority automated assessment tools are based on accessibility guidelines WCAG 2.0.

The use of web accessibility evaluation tools is a widespread practice. Evaluation tools are heavily employed as they help in reducing the burden of identifying accessibility barriers. However, an overreliance on automated tests often leads to setting aside further testing that entails expert evaluation and user tests [15].
The tools used in this evaluation are TAW and Examinator.

A. TAW The web accessibility evaluation was performed with Test of Accessibility Web (TAW), an online tool developed by the Unit Web Accessibility of Foundation CTIC (Centre for Information and Communication Technology). This tool allows analyze automatically the accessibility of websites. TAW comprehensively revises all the items and pages that compose the website. In the report these are detailed three parts:

Part 1: header shows the logo, the version of the standard Web Accessibility Initiative (WAI) Part 2: Analyzed Web, displays icons alert on accessibility issues found Part 3: Summary, are published, problems accessibility found, organized by priority, indicates the code of the verification point, description of the problem, line number of the page analyzed, HTML tag that generates the problem of accessibility. TAW automatically validates the accessibility of the site and it indicates the checkpoints to be checked manually.

V. CONCLUSIONS This paper concludes that the majority of tested websites do not conform an acceptable level of compliance. Universities with high academic prestige have not been concerned to provide accessible information about the university through its website, so that, everyone can access it, regardless if the user has any disability.

None of the analyzed websites of prestigious universities worldwide accomplished accessibility guidelines; therefore, their pages are hardly accessible [16]. By performing the evaluation of universities websites, we have identified that there are major barriers to a large number of users.

The identified barriers may hinder or prevent access to contents to people who may have a physical or sensorial limitation. Web pages should offer several alternatives, different presentations, to suit the needs of most users and they should be replicable under different circumstances. This study has limitations and has taken risks in the planning stage, but can serve as lessons learned for future work.
Future research may highlight the best methods for implementing the guidelines of WCAG 2.0 into existing websites specially to redevelop a website more inclusive for users.

div.head: B. Examinator
div.p: It is an online service that automatically evaluates the accessibility of a web page, using as a reference some 4 Without to apply the tool recommended of WCAG 2.0. Examinator adjudges a score between 1 and 10 as indicator of the accessibility of the pages and provides a detailed report of the tests performed. The highest score upon in the range of ten indicates that the website is more accessible.

TABLE V shows the universities has a score of 8, which corresponds to an acceptable average level and those are the universities of Stanford and Queensland. The largest group between 5 and less than 7.9 corresponds to an average acceptable level. This is awarded to Harvard University, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Universidade Estadual de Campinas, Universidad de Chile, University of Oxford, University of Cambridge, University College London, University of Tokyo, National Taiwan University, Stellenbosch University, University of Pretoria, University of Melbourne and the University of New South Wales. The universities that has a lower score, less than five. In those universities are Universidade de São Paulo USP, Peking University and University of Cape Town.
The automatic review cannot cover all compliance criteria of WCAG 2.0. For evaluation and manual analysis is necessary to have the assistance of an expert [15].
